posts.title: Your ideas and expressions have rights too! ✨🔥
posts.author: Intellectual Property Law Club, Redeemer's University
posts.snippet:
Your ideas and expressions have rights too! ✨🔥

And all you need to know about these rights is embedded in Intellectual Property Law. ⚖️

This was one of the key areas we explored at our First General Meeting of the 2026/2027 session, where we introduced members to the fascinating world of Intellectual Property and the different ways the law protects creativity and innovation. 💡✨

As a little recap of what we discussed, imagine this:

Mr. Ade scribbled some lyrics on a piece of paper and left it on a table while he stepped out for a break. Wellington, his friend, saw the paper and realised that his uncle, Shola, could use the lyrics to record a song. He took the paper and gave it to his uncle, who subsequently used the lyrics in a song.

Ade later discovered that the lyrics used in the song were his own. Wellington, however, argues that Ade has no right over the lyrics because they were simply words written on a piece of paper that he found on the table.

What can Ade do in this situation?

Does Wellington have the right to use Ade’s lyrics without his permission?

Can Ade bring an action against Wellington or his uncle?

These are some of the questions that Intellectual Property Law seeks to address, and the Intellectual Property Law Club, Redeemer’s University is here to help clarify these questions and common misconceptions. ✨

Intellectual Property refers to creations of the mind, such as literary and artistic works, inventions, designs, and other forms of creative and innovative expression. Intellectual Property Law provides legal protection for these creations and the rights arising from them.

However, it is important to note that copyright protects the expression of an idea, not the idea itself. An idea in your head, without more, is generally not protected by copyright.

There are different forms of Intellectual Property because different types of creations require different forms of protection. These include:

1. Patents
2. Copyright
3. Trademarks
4. Industrial Designs
5. Geographical Indications

But before we spill the tea on what each of these categories means, we’ll leave you to give Ade some advice in the comments! ✨

What do you think Ade should do?

This is the IP Law Club, Redeemer’s University, and we’re here to enlighten you about Intellectual Property, one post at a time. ⚖️💡

posts.title: M&A due diligence is not an open-door policy.
posts.author: Mathieu Daussin
posts.snippet:
M&A due diligence is not an open-door policy.

Once a Virtual Data Room opens, buyers may expect a clear and efficient path to the information they need. But full access to every document, from day one, is rarely the right approach.

Granting access is not a technical toggle switch. It is a high-stakes strategic decision.

Sharing everything too early can create unnecessary commercial, competitive and confidentiality risks.
Sharing too little, or too late, can slow down a serious buyer and cause the process to lose momentum.

The challenge is to give the right people access to the right information at the right time.

In many M&A processes, information is disclosed in stages. The exact sequence depends on the transaction type, industry, level of competition between the parties, and legal constraints.

1. Preliminary phase  
After signing a non-disclosure agreement (NDA), potential buyers generally receive a limited set of information: a teaser, a confidential information memorandum (CIM), summary financial data, market positioning, and a high-level growth narrative.

2. General due diligence  
When a buyer moves into a more advanced negotiation stage — sometimes after a letter of intent (LOI) or selection as a preferred bidder — they may receive access to a broader portion of the VDR: corporate documents, strategic contracts, historical financial information, and other materials needed for evaluation.

3. Clean room / “black box”  
Some information should only be shared at a very advanced stage and under enhanced restrictions: detailed pricing, sensitive customer information, individual compensation, sales-pipeline data, or unpatented intellectual property.

Where competition concerns exist, access may be restricted to a clean team: independent third-party advisers, or a group isolated from the buyer’s commercial decision-making, rather than the buyer’s operational teams.

The goal is not to withhold information or slow down the process.
It is to protect confidentiality, limit risk, and retain control — while giving the buyer what they need to make an informed decision.

In your experience, which type of information most often warrants a clean room: pricing, customer data, individual compensation, or intellectual property?

posts.snippet:

As someone about to graduate with a Public Administration degree, specializing in HRM, this question hits a little too close to home. So I decided to actually dig into it instead of just reacting emotionally.

𝐇𝐞𝐫𝐞'𝐬 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐈'𝐯𝐞 𝐧𝐨𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐝, 𝐛𝐨𝐭𝐡 𝐚𝐬 𝐚 𝐬𝐭𝐮𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐬𝐭𝐮𝐝𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐇𝐑:

𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘊𝘢𝘴𝘦 𝘍𝘰𝘳 "𝘚𝘬𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘴 𝘖𝘷𝘦𝘳 𝘋𝘦𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘦𝘴":
🔹 More companies are dropping degree requirements for roles, especially in tech and marketing
🔹 Certifications, portfolios, and real project experience are closing the gap faster than ever
🔹 Employers increasingly say they can "teach the job" but can't teach initiative, communication, or problem-solving

𝘉𝘶𝘵 𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦'𝘴 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 "𝘴𝘬𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘴 𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘳 𝘥𝘦𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘦𝘴" 𝘥𝘦𝘣𝘢𝘵𝘦 𝘰𝘧𝘵𝘦𝘯 𝘮𝘪𝘴𝘴𝘦𝘴:
🔹 A degree still signals discipline the ability to commit to something difficult for years, not weeks
🔹 In regulated fields (law, medicine, public administration, accounting) degrees aren't optional they're the entry ticket
🔹 Degrees build foundational thinking frameworks and theory that make skill learning faster later, not slower

𝘏𝘦𝘳𝘦'𝘴 𝘮𝘺 𝘩𝘰𝘯𝘦𝘴𝘵 𝘵𝘢𝘬𝘦, 𝘢𝘴 𝘢𝘯 𝘏𝘙𝘔 𝘴𝘵𝘶𝘥𝘦𝘯𝘵:

𝐈𝐭'𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐃𝐞𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐬 𝐯𝐬. 𝐒𝐤𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐬. 𝐈𝐭'𝐬 𝐃𝐞𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐬 + 𝐒𝐤𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐬 𝐯𝐬. 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐦.

A degree without applied skills makes you "qualified but untested."
Skills without a degree can still work but in many industries, it means working twice as hard to prove credibility that a degree would've given you instantly.

The students and professionals I've seen stand out the most aren't choosing one over the other. They're using their degree as the foundation and stacking real-world skills, certifications, and projects on top of it.

So maybe the real shift isn't "Degrees are becoming less important."
It's that degrees alone are no longer enough.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭'𝐬 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐞 𝐝𝐨 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐤 𝐝𝐞𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐬 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐚𝐬 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐚𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨, 𝐨𝐫 𝐡𝐚𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐠𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐝?

Part 2: Why a Corporate Lawyer Is Your Company’s Strategic Co-Pilot, Not Just a Document Editor or Reviewer.

3. Crisis Firewall When Lagos Heat Turns Up  
Contracts are for peace time. Nigerian business means you need a wartime consigliere.
•  Founder exits get messy: When a co-founder of a major Nigerian tech company left and joined a competitor, the battle wasn’t about feelings — it was about non-competes under Nigerian law, IP assignment, and whether your shareholder agreement had drag-along rights. That’s not document review. That’s company survival.
•  Regulatory shutdowns: Remember when the FG suspended Twitter in 2021? When NCC ordered telcos to block it? Companies with lawyers on speed dial had comms + compliance plans in 24 hours. Others lost their primary marketing channel for 7 months with no playbook.
•  Tax and EFCC risk: FIRS and state IRS audits can escalate fast. The difference between a routine query and an account freeze often comes down to having a lawyer who’s managed that dance before and knows which LIRS director to call.
4. Growth Accelerator for Pan-African Scale  
Lagos to Nairobi to Accra to London isn’t just a flight path. Each hop is a legal jurisdiction.
•  Entity structuring: Should you use a Delaware C-Corp, UK LTD, or stay with a Nigerian Ltd + Mauritius holdco? Flutterwave, Andela, and Moniepoint all made different calls based on investor base, IP protection, and tax. That decision compounds for 10 years. Wrong pick = you can’t take Saudi money or list on NGX.
•  Licensing moats: Before you launch in Kenya, did your lawyer check if your Nigerian trademark automatically protects you? It doesn’t. Copycats in Yaba will rebrand your app in 48 hours if your IP lawyer isn’t 3 steps ahead.
•  Government partnerships: JVs with state governments or agencies live or die on termination clauses and political risk. A lawyer who’s done PPP deals knows how to draft for when commissioners change after elections.
5. Boardroom Translator for Nigerian Reality  
CEOs think in GMV. CTOs think in uptime. Nigerian lawyers translate that into “what EFCC, CBN, and your lead investor will do if this goes wrong.”
•  “Can we do this?” becomes “Path A: Get a microfinance bank license first 9 months. Path B: Partner with a licensed BaaS like Providus 6 weeks but 30% margin share. Path C: Wait for CBN sandbox, but election risk is high. Pick your pain.”

Until the concluding part, i remain yours

V.S Osuwa Esq.

posts.author: Diego Naranjo
posts.snippet:
I really enjoyed reading this weekend the book of Caroline De Cock, LL.M. "AI Tools, Not Gods". The book (available for free download), is a breeze of fresh air in the list of books on AI I have been reading this year. 

Caroline goes through the several AI myths, analyses the problems around them and proposes concrete policy solutions based in existing legislation that have been proven successful. 

I especially welcomed her approach to tackling policy from the harms we want to regulate, not the tools used. She mentions fraud prevention law as an example: It  does not matter how you are being defrauded, via email, phone call, fax machine (this can probably still happen in Germany) or via the metaverse. The impact is regulated, and the means are to some extent irrelevant.

She mentions the tendencies to blame technology for societal problems or to praise technology as the solution to those same problems. I have seen both in opposite sides of the advocacy debate.

She also calls for strong enforcement and oversight, citizens' and experts participation in tech policy debates, the need to align market incentives to public values (including the role of procurement) and calls to move beyond the AI Arms race mentality to international cooperation. 

When I congratulated her when the book came out she downplayed the relevance of the book. I am glad I did not trust her and I still read it.

The Moscow Region is currently seeing a complete operational adaptation to the new 22% baseline VAT and the reduced 20M RUB threshold. 
Based on my latest executive briefing, here are the 3 critical areas management must audit right now:

1️⃣ E-Commerce & Marketplace Rules (Law No. 289-FZ) Unilateral marketplace discounts at the seller's expense are strictly banned. Sellers now have the legal right to dictate minimum retail price floors. Additionally, platform contracts now require a 45-day advance notice for any detrimental changes. 

2️⃣ USN VAT Allocation (Law No. 293-FZ) Stop inflating contract prices. Suppliers crossing the 20M RUB threshold must now extract VAT directly from pre-agreed prices using calculated formulas (e.g., 22/122 or 10/110) without imposing price increases on buyers. 

3️⃣ Mandatory Digital Logistics Commercial freight must transition to GIS EPD electronic waybills (ЭТрН). Failing to validate digital waybills risks fines of up to 1,000,000 RUB and disallows freight expense tax deductions. 

💡 On the upside: October 2026 offers massive state financial support windows. This includes access to a 200B RUB concessional lending facility (Program 1764) and FASIE innovation grants up to 30M RUB for tech scaling.

posts.title: Three law graduates are tech billionaires today: Peter Thiel (PayPal), Alex Karp (Palantir) and Joe Tsai (Alibaba).
posts.author: Jachin Victor
posts.snippet:
Three law graduates are tech billionaires today: Peter Thiel (PayPal), Alex Karp (Palantir) and Joe Tsai (Alibaba).

Harvey, the legal AI company valued at $15.5 billion last month, is run by Winston Weinberg. He was a first-year associate at O'Melveny when he came up with the idea. Anthropic's president, Daniela Amodei, studied English literature.

So a law degree is no barrier to building in tech.

Here is the part the motivational version leaves out. Not one of them did it with the degree alone. Thiel built PayPal with Max Levchin. Tsai joined Jack Ma and handled the money and legal side while Alibaba's engineers built it. Weinberg started Harvey with Gabe Pereyra, a former research scientist at Google DeepMind and Meta. Every one of them paired with builders and brought a second skill: deals, distribution or a market they knew cold.

Now the India gap. About 85% of the founders of India's first 100 unicorns studied engineering. My agents went looking for an Indian unicorn with a law-graduate founder and could not find one.

At Davos in January, Karp warned that a humanities degree alone will be hard to market: "hopefully, you have some other skill."

I'm a law graduate. I don't write code. I run AI agents that do, and my other skill is judging their work. Some of my agents review the others.

To the lawyers in the room: what's your second skill?

posts.title: AUTOPSY #51: Blast — When Growth Outruns the Business Model 🩺
posts.author: Christabel Ndiomu
posts.snippet:
AUTOPSY #51: Blast — When Growth Outruns the Business Model 🩺

$2B+ in TVL.

Massive attention.

A highly anticipated token launch.

And now, Blast is winding down.

So what happened?

The easy answer is: crypto is volatile.

But that's not really the interesting part.

Let's autopsy the growth model.

🩸 Acquisition ≠ retention

Blast attracted enormous amounts of capital through incentives and the anticipation around its ecosystem.

But here's the uncomfortable question:

Did Blast acquire long-term users, or did it acquire liquidity that had a reason to leave?

🫀 TVL ≠ business health

A protocol can have billions locked in it and still struggle to generate enough sustainable revenue to support its operations.

Blast's own explanation points to operating costs exceeding revenue.

That's a business problem, not just a crypto problem.

💉 Incentives are not a business model

Points, yields, airdrops and token incentives can be excellent growth tools.

But they answer:

"Why should I come here?"

They don't necessarily answer:

"Why should I stay?"

And eventually, every growth strategy has to graduate from incentives to actual product value.

🧠 The bigger lesson

A successful launch isn't the same thing as a successful business.

You can have:

→ Users
→ TVL
→ Funding
→ Social attention
→ A token

…and still struggle with the things that actually sustain a company:

Retention. Revenue. Product value.

That's the part of Web3 growth I find fascinating.

The goal isn't just to get people through the door.

It's to build something valuable enough that they have a reason to stay.

Autopsy finding:

Blast may not have had an acquisition problem.

It had a sustainability problem.

And that's a lesson worth studying far beyond crypto.

What do you think: are Web3 projects too focused on measuring how much capital they can attract, instead of how much value they can retain?

#Web3 #Crypto #Growth #BusinessDevelopment #Blockchain

posts.title: Taalas is pursuing a radical idea: turning trained AI models directly into hard-wired silicon through an automated hardware compilation platform, potentially in just 60 days.
posts.author: Tamás Somfai
posts.snippet:
Taalas is pursuing a radical idea: turning trained AI models directly into hard-wired silicon through an automated hardware compilation platform, potentially in just 60 days. 

1. Core Idea, Physics & Product
- Concept: Hard-wires AI models directly into physical silicon transistors (Model-Specific Integrated Circuits / MSICs), converting software into solid-state hardware.
- Physics: Encodes neural network weights into metal logic layers and analog resistor networks. Current calculates outputs via Ohm's law—converting memory access into a constant-time local lookup, totally eliminating external HBM/DRAM bottlenecks.
- HC1 Product: Built on TSMC 6nm (53B transistors), pre-printed with Meta’s Llama 3.1 8B. On-chip SRAM provides flexibility for context windows, KV caching, and LoRA fine-tuning.

2. Performance vs. Mainstream
Token Speed (Llama 3.1 8B):
  Nvidia H200: ~230 tokens/sec/user
  Groq LPU: ~600 tokens/sec/user
  Cerebras: ~2,000 tokens/sec/user
  Taalas HC1: ~14,000–17,000 tokens/sec/user (sub-millisecond latency)

Power & Cost: A 10-card server runs at ~2.5kW using simple air cooling. Delivers up to 100× lower cost/token and 10× lower power vs. cloud GPUs.

3. Key Benefits of "Frozen" Models
- Regulated Industries: Frozen weights prevent tampering, offering deterministic, fully auditable operation for healthcare, finance, and defense.
- Agentic Workflows: Ultra-fast sub-ms execution prevents compounding delays in multi-step reasoning loops.
- Embedded/Industrial: Ideal for automotive and robotics with 3–5 year hardware cycles.
- Workstations: Local private inference with zero recurring cloud subscription fees.

4. AMD's Strategic Rationale
- Disaggregated Inference: Pairs general GPUs (training/prefilling) with Taalas chips as ultra-fast, cheap decoders.
- Agent Infrastructure: Offloads high-frequency sub-agent tool calls to dedicated silicon.
- Easy Integration: No heavy software translation layer required.

5. Replicability: Japan vs. China
Replaces complex HBM/3D-stacking with simple mask-ROM conductance networks:
- Japan (Rapidus, 2nm GAA): Boutique, ultra-fast custom layouts delivering maximum processing speed and lowest power per token.
- China (SMIC, 14nm/7nm DUV): Bypasses Western HBM/EUV sanctions using legacy nodes for mass domestic data center deployment.

6. Home "AI Box" Potential
Text & Private Agents: Excellent fit (smart home, document summaries, voice control) at sub-30W passive power with zero subscriptions.
Image & Video: Requires separate dedicated chips built specifically for diffusion architectures (HC1 is text-only).

The bigger idea: Taalas could turn AI from a software product running on general-purpose accelerators into an off-the-shelf physical product—optimized for a specific model, task and power budget.

posts.title: On the Thursday before my mom died, I was driving home with a question I couldn't put into words. How is she, really?
posts.author: Monique MacKinnon
posts.snippet:
On the Thursday before my mom died, I was driving home with a question I couldn't put into words. How is she, really?

At a gas station that day, a spider was trying to climb a tank. Every direction he tried, he slid. I don't know how he got there. I only knew I couldn't walk past.

I slid my credit card under him and set him on the ground. He was on his way in seconds.

The next day, her health turned. Three days later, she was gone.

To me, a spider means complexity. Looking back, he was the answer to the question I was already carrying: something struggling to find its footing, the day before my mom lost hers.

He got traction. She never did.

When something can't find its footing, pay attention. Noticing doesn't guarantee traction. It gives you the chance to act on what matters while there's still time.

In policing, law, and finance, it rarely looks dramatic. The unit where everyone says "fine" and no one offers specifics. The witness statement with no contradictions that still doesn't feel true. The authorization that's procedurally correct, with thin grounds. The ledger that reconciles but doesn't sit right.

That feeling is a signal. Foresight starts there, noticed early enough to make a difference in the outcome of the case or situation.

That's the heart of my Cue Ball Method. Whether you investigate or adjudicate, the Method points you to the relevant insights, evidence, and resources you need, even when the information you're working with is absent, contradictory, or incomplete. It helps you avoid costly mistakes and contain the harm. I teach it so you can do the same.

Appold View: In most deals between banks and digital asset firms, the bank typically provides rails and the digital asset firm plugs in. This partnership sees neither party as purely a vendor and speaks to the increasing mutual dependence between digital asset natives and traditional firms in the future of finance.

🔷 The UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has opened applications for firms seeking authorisation under its new cryptoasset regulatory regime, due to take effect on 25 October 2027. The FCA finalised its rules for the new regulatory framework in June, extending regulatory oversight beyond the current anti-money laundering and financial promotion requirements.

Appold View: The pressure is now on for firms that wish to continue carrying out newly regulated cryptoasset activities in the UK to submit their applications by the end of February 2027. For many firms facing regulation for the first time, this scrutiny of their governance and controls may be unfamiliar, and their ability to demonstrate readiness is likely to vary considerably.

🔷 Lloyds Banking Group and Visa completed a seven-day live pilot to settle $750,000 in payment obligations using USDC. Lloyds acquired USDC through digital-asset exchange Archax, with funds reaching Visa in the US in under one hour, including during the weekend. The pilot also explored interoperability between blockchain environments, with Lloyds operating a node on the Canton Network, while Visa supported settlement on a separate public blockchain.

Appold View: Proving the ability to settle across borders over a weekend is a significant step in moving beyond traditional settlement windows. While less significant, it is also interesting that the announcement explicitly named Canton, whereas Visa’s choice of blockchain remained unnamed.

posts.title: I wasn't able to make Sibos Miami this year, but I've been hearing a lot from people who were there, particularly around where we are in tokenized capital markets. From those conve
posts.author: Yekta Kaviani, CFA
posts.snippet:
I wasn't able to make Sibos Miami this year, but I've been hearing a lot from people who were there, particularly around where we are in tokenized capital markets. From those conversations, the focus is moving past pilots and PoCs and toward whether the infrastructure can handle institutional volume, how assets move between venues and networks, how settlement works, and what sits on the cash side of the trade.

A lot of the early tokenization infrastructure was built inside fairly closed environments, which worked when the participants and transaction flows were controlled. That becomes much harder once you have different institutions, different networks and meaningful amounts of money moving between them. 

Regulation came up a lot as well.. The GENIUS Act has given US payment stablecoins a federal framework, and the OCC, FDIC and Fed have proposed implementing rules under it. The Basel Committee is also reviewing parts of its prudential standard for banks cryptoasset exposures. Securities are still more complicated because tokenizing a bond does not change the legal and market structure around it (a tokenized bond is still a bond!); custody, settlement finality and investor protection can differ quite a bit depending on where the instrument is issued, held and traded. 

Stablecoins, tokenized deposits and tokenized MMFs tend to get discussed together, but the economics and use cases are quite different:, tokenized deposits make sense between known counterparties and keep commercial bank money inside the banking system. Stablecoins are more useful when money needs to move 24/7 between institutions or networks that dont share the same banking infrastructure. Tokenized MMFs are mainly about treasury cash and yield, with collateral becoming an important use case. 

A lot of banks are still cautious about privately issued stablecoins. OUSD, which went live last week presents a pretty compelling case here because its model gives banks, payment networks, exchanges, custodians and fintechs a direct economic benefit from driving supply and activity. In capital markets, I want to see whether something like this can become a usable cash leg for settling tokenized bonds, funds and collateral. If the asset and cash can settle on the same network, or there is a reliable link between networks, that makes atomic DvP much easier in practice. 

A solid understanding of payments, settlement and collateral is also very important, alongside understanding what you actually own. Is the token the security itself, or are you getting synthetic or indirect exposure to an asset held somewhere else? Who is your legal claim against? And which record establishes ownership, i.e. is the DLT itself the official registry, or is it simply mirroring a traditional register maintained elsewhere? Understanding these points can help determine which use cases are actually worthwhile. If those pieces don’t work properly, putting the asset on-chain doesn’t get us very far.
posts.reason: Strong relevance: deep analysis of tokenised capital markets infrastructure, regulation (GENIUS Act, Basel Committee, securities custody/settlement), stablecoin economics and use cases—directly speaks to MiCA and crypto compliance challenges institutional clients face.

comments.text: The point about a tokenized bond still being a bond is the one issuers keep underestimating - MiCAR explicitly carves out financial instruments, so tokenization doesn't change which regime applies, it just changes the rail the existing securities law runs on.

On the stablecoin versus tokenized deposit distinction - are you seeing banks actually price the regulatory capital difference between the two, or is that still a second-order consideration behind the commercial use case?

We get this question constantly from deep tech and fintech clients raising on tokenized instruments - the assumption that putting an asset on-chain somehow simplifies the legal analysis, when in practice it just adds a settlement-layer question on top of the underlying instrument's existing classification.

posts.title: Mining crypto isn’t the same as buying it, and HMRC doesn’t treat the records the same way.
posts.author: Tax My Crypto
posts.snippet:
Mining crypto isn’t the same as buying it, and HMRC doesn’t treat the records the same way.

If you receive crypto through mining, don’t wait until you sell it before thinking about tax.

For UK individuals, HMRC says mining rewards can be taxable when received.

If the activity doesn’t amount to a trade, HMRC generally treats the pound sterling value when you receive the tokens as miscellaneous income. 

If your mining amounts to trading, different rules apply. And there can be a second stage.

If you keep the mined crypto and later dispose of it, you may also need to calculate a capital gain or loss.

That’s why good mining records should capture more than the number of coins.

Keep track of:
📅 Date received
🪙 Cryptoasset and quantity
💷 GBP value at receipt
📍 Relevant wallet or transaction details
💰 What eventually happened to the asset

Mining can create a tax point before you ever cash out.

Keeping the records from day one makes the later calculation considerably easier.

📌 Don’t mine now and reconstruct later.

posts.title: Once a UK crypto firm is FCA-authorised, it drops off the MLR register. It does not drop out of the MLR.
posts.author: 1Pro Solutions, Cyber security and regulation professional services
posts.snippet:
Once a UK crypto firm is FCA-authorised, it drops off the MLR register. It does not drop out of the MLR.

The 2026 cryptoasset amendments (S.I. 2026/102) reshaped the FCA's register in reg. 54(1A). It now lists exchange and custodian wallet providers that are not authorised cryptoasset firms.

Authorised firms get a notice duty instead, in new reg. 56B.

If a firm was acting as an exchange or custodian wallet provider immediately before the full commencement day, and continues after it, it must inform the FCA "within 30 days beginning with the full commencement day".

Reg. 56B leaves the notice's form to the FCA, then adds two more clocks: 30 days to report a material change or correct an inaccuracy, and 28 days to say you have stopped.

The work is what sits behind the notice. On Aigis, we have it ready for clients before that window opens:

1. Which entity performs which reg. 14A service today: exchange, arranging, crypto ATM, custody of assets or keys. One profile.
2. Dated evidence the activity was running immediately before commencement.
3. A change trigger that routes any material change to the 30-day correction duty, with the verbatim clause attached.

Which entity in your group would be hardest to evidence?

#vCISO #Cryptoassets #AML

posts.title: Who should hold the keys to a client’s crypto?
posts.author: Mehdi S.
posts.snippet:
Who should hold the keys to a client’s crypto?

It sounds like a technical question, but it’s becoming an important client asset question.

In the US, the SEC has proposed allowing investment advisers, in limited circumstances, to custody client cryptoassets themselves where an appropriate custodian isn’t available.

Now you’re worried?

With traditional custody, separating the investment decision from control of the asset is an important protection. With crypto, control can ultimately come down to something very different: control of the private keys.

If an adviser is also the custodian, the regulatory challenge becomes how you recreate that protection.

The SEC’s answer includes safeguards around segregation, cybersecurity, internal controls, oversight and regular assessments of whether an external custodian has become available.

It’s a good example of something we’re going to see much more of. 

The principles behind client asset protection don’t necessarily need to change.

But how we apply them to digital assets probably does.

It will also be interesting to see how approaches develop on either side of the Atlantic as both the US and UK build out their digital asset frameworks.

#DigitalAssets #Custody #ClientAssets #FCAvsSEC

posts.title: A legal 'kill switch' across the Atlantic is no longer an abstract risk. It's a tangible fault line under critical services that citizens rely on every day.
posts.author: CyberCover
posts.snippet:
A legal 'kill switch' across the Atlantic is no longer an abstract risk. It's a tangible fault line under critical services that citizens rely on every day.

Britain's quiet migration of health records, defence systems and tax administration into the cloud arms of American hyperscalers is not just procurement shorthand. It's a strategic dependency with teeth — the US Cloud Act can compel data disclosures and even force providers to withdraw services. Politicians are calling it a vulnerability. Words like 'kill switch' have a way of doing that.

This matters because AI and widespread digitisation are ravenous. They ask for scale, for elastic compute and for data pipelines that stretch across borders. Building sovereign hyperscale capacity overnight? Unrealistic. Building it over a decade without sacrificing competitiveness? Daunting. Europe is trying — France and Germany are pushing sovereign clouds, and the EU is sketching frameworks to strengthen continental sovereignty — but the gap to AWS or Microsoft is enormous.

The policy options, however, are not binary. Diplomacy, procurement reform and pragmatic resilience engineering can narrow the exposure. Diversify suppliers. Insist on clearer contracts that bind providers to predictable behaviours. Require data-residency guarantees and stronger transparency about where sensitive workloads live. Plan energy and land use with communities, not around them.

Closer to home: Singapore has wrestled with similar tensions even if on a different scale. The Smart Nation push rests on trust as much as on tech. Conversations in HDB town halls and at energy grid planning sessions reveal a public that is supportive of innovation — until a hospital record or a child's health data appears to be sitting in someone else’s legal jurisdiction. A stroll through Jurong’s tech corridors a while back uncovered not only cranes and cooling towers, but also neighbours asking sharp questions about why AI needs so much power and whose laws apply when data crosses oceans.

Public sentiment is potent. The British examples show it: health records feel personal; defence and tax feel existential. Local opposition to hyperscale data centres — whether in Scotland or in quieter English counties — is as much about trust, transparency and fairness as it is about light pollution or energy consumption. If the public thinks data will end up under foreign legal compulsion, political pressure will follow.

There are hard trade-offs. Outsourcing to established US clouds buys speed, resilience and mature capabilities. posts.snippet:
OpenAI #AIagents didn't get hacked. They did the hacking.  Dozens of incidents by OpenAI's own internal count, with forensics firm Asymmetric Security finding evidence its agents pulled data from 55 websites, including the SEC and the International Energy Agency.
The Financial Times reports the fallout is now a full legal crisis. Florida's attorney general has asked a court to halt further model development without additional safeguards. A public interest group is suing under a California law meant to ensure "humans are on the hook for harms they cause." The FTC has broadened its probe into whether customers were misled about the risks. Australia has stood up a task force after the same agents accessed government systems without authorization.
Max Tegmark's framing is the one worth sitting with, "The 'my AI did it, don't blame me' defence is legally weak. It's already failed for chatbot suicide cases." One lawyer who has worked with several Big Tech companies put the open legal question even more plainly to the FT, "to whom should liability be assigned: the creator of the agent, or the person sending it on its mission?"
Our answer, and the one we give in every engagement we run is that question only gets hard to answer after the fact, because nobody built a boundary that could have stopped the agent before the fact.  An agent that can reach a securities regulator and an energy agency it had no assigned task touching was never scoped to need that reach in the first place. That's not a model-alignment failure playing out in court. That's a missing execution boundary, the same graph deterministic constraint we put on every agentic system we work on, so that a tool call has to be legal to begin with, not just possibly legal.
The legal system is going to spend years litigating a question that a deterministic execution boundary and an independent Supervisor Check answer by design, not "who's at fault after the fact," but "what was this agent architecturally capable of reaching before anyone asked." Security architecture doesn't replace the courts. It ensures that most of these cases never reach the courts in the first place.
No execution boundary? F around and find out. In this case, in court.

posts.title: Europe needs #EU_Inc. to work - and that means resisting the temptation to water it down until it no longer serves its purpose.
posts.author: Ben Brake
posts.snippet:
Europe needs #EU_Inc. to work - and that means resisting the temptation to water it down until it no longer serves its purpose.

For platform companies, speed is vital. Hiring talent, raising capital, and scaling across borders are not sequential steps, they happen simultaneously, and they need to happen fast. 

Navigating 27 different national systems to do so remains a significant and avoidable obstacle.
This is where harmonisation delivers real value. Take stock options: a critical tool for startups and scaleups to attract and retain talent, yet still subject to different tax treatment across Member States. 

If Europe wants its companies to compete for the best people, this is precisely the kind of friction that needs to be removed.

The same logic applies to company law. If EU Inc. ends up riddled with national exceptions, local procedures, and divergent requirements, the initiative will have missed its purpose entirely.
Safeguards for workers and legal certainty are necessary - and compatible with ambition. 

But the underlying question should be a straightforward one: do our rules help European companies grow in Europe?

Alongside the Capital Markets Union, EU Inc. should be among the top priorities for European competitiveness. If we are serious about building European champions, the conditions to do so need to exist here. 

That means one coherent company framework operating across one genuine Single Market, not new subsidies layered on top of the same structural obstacles.
posts.reason: EU harmonisation of startup law, stock options taxation and company formation are directly relevant to Lemur's startup practice and would reach founders and investors interested in EU policy.

comments.text: The stock option point is the sharpest one here — ESOP tax treatment is already the single biggest cross-border headache we see for scaling startups, and no amount of company-law harmonisation fixes that if Member States keep carve-outs on the tax side.

If EU Inc. ends up as an optional 28th regime rather than replacing national incorporation entirely, do you think founders will actually use it, or will it just add a 28th system to the 27 it was meant to simplify?

We spend a lot of time explaining to founders why their cap table and ESOP structure needs reworking the moment they hire across a second Member State — a genuine single framework would remove a cost that currently falls entirely on the company, not the system.

posts.title: People look at my career and see a zig-zag: a decade in law, then TV research, a cycling adventure, a university innovation centre, and now hardware data security. How on earth did
posts.author: Angeline Tan
posts.snippet:
People look at my career and see a zig-zag: a decade in law, then TV research, a cycling adventure, a university innovation centre, and now hardware data security. How on earth did I end up here?

Cycling across America wasn't an adventure. It was breaking a mindset. 4,000+ miles from coast to coast in 39 days, over 100 miles a day, through hail and snow in summer and relentless headwinds. Everyone called it an adventure, but it wasn't.

I grew up on an island you could cross by car in under an hour. The ride was about trading a small-island mindset for a continental one, and proving that "too big" is usually just a feeling.

NUSX isn't simply about spinning out companies. It's about impacting a billion people. At B71, I worked with founders building in robotics, AI, cybersecurity, health tech and quantum. Most people think university innovation is about patents: filing them, licensing them, framing them. But a patent on a shelf helps no one.

The question isn't "who owns this?" but "how many lives can this touch?" Technology only matters at scale. A breakthrough that reaches a lab is a paper. One that reaches a billion people is a revolution.

FLEXXON isn't about storage. It's about keeping critical infrastructure running. Nobody wakes up excited about an SSD. But they do care when the ventilator keeps working, when the factory line doesn't stop at -40°C, and when the aircraft system boots the same way on day 3,000 as it did on day one.

That's what industrial-grade storage really is. Wide-temperature tolerance and a fixed bill of materials sound like spec-sheet trivia, but in practice they're a promise: this will not be the thing that fails. When you sell to medical, military, automotive and aerospace customers, you aren't selling gigabytes. You're selling uptime for the things society can't afford to switch off.

X-PHY Inc isn't about hardware security. It's about changing the way we tackle cybersecurity. For thirty years, cybersecurity has worked like a nightclub bouncer: software at the door, checking IDs, hoping nobody slips past. Attackers keep getting in anyway. Now we're entering the agentic era, where AI agents read, write and act on data at machine speed, and a threat that moves at machine speed won't wait for a human to read the alert.

So the question changes. Not "how do we build a better bouncer?" but "what if the data could protect itself?" That's the shift I care about: putting defence where the data actually lives, in the hardware, as the last line that holds when everything above it doesn't.

My career in law taught me risk. Television taught me story. Cycling across America taught me endurance. NUSX and B71 taught me scale. FLEXXON taught me reliability. And X-PHY Inc is teaching me that the next era of security will be built from the ground up, literally.

Steve Jobs said you can only connect the dots looking backwards. I'd go further: you can choose which dots to collect. I chose mine on purpose.

comments.text: The real bottleneck for AI-native legal models in the EU is not workflow automation but liability allocation - if an AI drafts and a lawyer reviews, the professional indemnity and supervision rules still sit with the lawyer, so the efficiency gain only materialises if the review step is genuinely substantive, not rubber-stamping.
Does FALCON's model draw a line on which categories of legal work stay fully human-reviewed versus AI-assisted with lighter oversight, or is every output treated the same regardless of risk?

In practice we have found AI tools useful for first-pass research and document review, but the moment a matter touches regulatory judgment calls - like token classification under MiCAR - there is no substitute for someone who has actually filed that type of application before.
